title: 22. Interview: Indexing
summary: Interview Q&A for Indexing — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Indexing interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. How does a B-tree index work, and why is it the default index type?
**Answer:** A B-tree (balanced tree) is a sorted, multi-level tree where every leaf is at the same depth. The root and interior pages contain key values that partition the key space — e.g., a root with keys `[m, t, z]` routes lookups for `amy` to the leftmost child, `paul` to the middle, `xavier` to the right. Leaf pages contain sorted (key, tuple-ID) entries and are linked sideways (a doubly-linked list in most implementations) so range scans can walk efficiently. For a billion-row table, the tree is typically 3–4 levels deep, so any lookup is 3–4 page reads — O(log N). B-trees are the default because they support the widest range of operations: equality (`=`), range (`<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`), prefix matching (`LIKE 'abc%'`), and ordered output (`ORDER BY`). Hash indexes only support equality; bitmap indexes are for low-cardinality columns; GIN/GiST are for full-text and JSONB. The B-tree's balance property guarantees O(log N) regardless of insert order, and self-balancing on inserts/deletes keeps the tree efficient over time. Almost every `WHERE col = ?` or `WHERE col BETWEEN ? AND ?` query is served by a B-tree.
**Visual:**
```
B-tree on users.email (sorted, balanced):

         root: [ keys: m, t, z ]
        /        |         \
    [a..m]    [n..t]    [u..z]
      |          |          |
   leaf: alan, amy, ann    <- entries sorted, linked sideways
                  |
                  v
            (key='amy@x.com', tid=88)

Lookup 'amy@x.com': root (m>t? no) -> [a..m] -> leaf -> found -> tid=88
Total: 3 reads (vs 1B for sequential scan)
```

### Q2. What is the difference between an index scan and an index-only scan?
**Answer:** An **index scan** uses the index to find matching tuple IDs, then fetches each row from the heap (table storage) to read columns not present in the index. So per matching row: one index page read + one heap page read = two I/Os (potentially random). An **index-only scan** answers the query entirely from the index, with no heap fetch — possible only when every column the query needs (in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY) is present in the index. PostgreSQL also requires the visibility map to confirm the page is visible to all transactions (otherwise it must fetch the heap to check visibility). The performance difference is significant: index-only scans halve the I/O and avoid random heap access, which matters most when the heap is large and not cached. The trade-off is index size — including extra columns bloats the index, costing storage and write time. The standard pattern is to identify the top hot queries and build covering indexes for them (via PostgreSQL's `INCLUDE` clause, which adds non-key columns to the leaf without affecting the B-tree's sort order).
**Visual:**
```
Index scan:           index -> tid=88 -> heap fetch -> read full row
                      (2 I/Os per row: 1 index + 1 heap, random)

Index-only scan:      index -> tid + url + caption all in leaf -> return
                      (1 I/O per row: index only; no heap touch)

Requires: all SELECT/WHERE/ORDER BY cols in the index + visibility map clean.
Trade-off: larger index (storage + write cost) for faster reads.
```

### Q3. Why do indexes slow down writes, and how do you decide how many to have?
**Answer:** Every index adds an entry per row, so an INSERT must write to the table heap *and* to every index on the table. A table with 10 indexes pays 11 writes per INSERT (1 heap + 10 indexes), and similarly for UPDATEs and DELETEs on indexed columns. Additionally, B-tree pages can split on insert, causing write amplification; InnoDB's change buffer mitigates this for non-unique secondary indexes by deferring updates, but the cost is still real. The decision rule: index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses of queries that actually run in production — and remove indexes that aren't being used. PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` shows how often each index has been used; an index with `idx_scan = 0` over a representative period is dead weight. For write-heavy tables (metrics, logs, events), be especially parsimonious — often just the primary key and one or two lookup indexes suffice. For read-heavy tables (user profiles, product catalogs), more indexes are fine because the write cost is amortized over many reads. The sweet spot is usually 3–7 indexes per table; beyond that, write performance degrades noticeably.
**Visual:**
```
INSERT into a table with 4 indexes:
  heap write  +  idx1 write  +  idx2 write  +  idx3 write  +  idx4 write
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                5x write cost vs no indexes

Audit with:  SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes;
             idx_scan = 0 over a week  -> DROP INDEX (it's dead weight)

Sweet spot: 3-7 indexes per table; more for read-heavy, fewer for write-heavy.
```

### Q4. When does the optimizer choose a sequential scan over an index scan, and why?
**Answer:** The optimizer chooses a sequential scan when the predicate matches a large fraction of the table — typically above ~5–20% of rows. The reason is I/O pattern: an index scan does random I/O (one heap fetch per matching row, scattered across the table), while a sequential scan does sequential I/O (read every page in order). Sequential I/O is 10–100× faster than random I/O on spinning disks and still 2–10× faster on SSDs. So for a predicate matching 50% of rows, the sequential scan reads every page once (sequential), while the index scan reads the index (sequential within the index) plus one random heap fetch per matching row — net slower. The optimizer's cost model estimates selectivity from column statistics (most common values, histogram, distinct count); if it estimates the predicate matches 1% but it actually matches 50%, it picks an index scan that's 10× slower than a sequential scan. The fix is `ANALYZE` (refresh statistics) or extended statistics for correlated columns. Bitmap scans are the middle ground: the index lookup produces a bitmap of matching tuple IDs, which is then sorted by page number before heap fetches, converting random I/O into mostly-sequential I/O.
**Visual:**
```
Predicate matches X% of rows:
  X < 5%:    index scan wins       (random I/O, few heap fetches)
  5-20%:     bitmap scan wins      (index -> sorted bitmap -> batched heap)
  X > 20%:   sequential scan wins  (sequential I/O, reads all pages once)

Misestimate:  stats say 1% match, actually 50% -> optimizer picks index scan
              -> 10x slower than seq scan  -> run ANALYZE to fix stats
```

### Q5. What is a bitmap scan, and when is it better than a plain index scan?
**Answer:** A **bitmap scan** is a two-phase index access: first, the index lookup produces a bitmap of tuple IDs matching the predicate (one bit per page, or per tuple, depending on precision); second, the heap fetches are done in page-number order, converting random I/O into mostly-sequential I/O. There are two variants: **Bitmap Index Scan** (builds the bitmap) and **Bitmap Heap Scan** (fetches the pages in sorted order). Bitmap scans shine when the predicate matches many rows (5–20% of the table) — too many for a plain index scan (which would do random I/O per row) but too few for a sequential scan (which reads every page). Bitmap scans also combine multiple indexes: `WHERE col_a = 1 AND col_b = 2` can bitmap-scan both indexes and AND the bitmaps, then fetch only the pages where both match — useful when no single composite index covers the predicate. The trade-off is the bitmap has limited precision (one bit per page, not per tuple), so the heap fetch must re-check the predicate on each row. For very selective predicates (<1% of rows), a plain index scan is faster because it skips the bitmap construction overhead.
**Visual:**
```
Plain index scan:    index -> tid list -> fetch each row (RANDOM I/O per row)
Bitmap heap scan:    index -> bitmap of pages -> fetch pages IN ORDER -> recheck
                     (mostly-sequential I/O; wins for 5-20% selectivity)

Multi-index AND:     bitmap(col_a=1) AND bitmap(col_b=2) -> fetch matching pages
                    (useful when no composite index on (col_a, col_b) exists)
```

### Q6. What is a hash index, and why is it rarely used in PostgreSQL?
**Answer:** A hash index stores keys in a hash table indexed by `hash(key)`, supporting only equality (`=`) lookups in O(1) average time. It cannot do range queries (`<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`), prefix matching (`LIKE 'abc%'`), or ordered output (`ORDER BY`) — those require a B-tree's sorted structure. Historically, PostgreSQL's hash indexes were not crash-safe (not replicated via WAL) before version 10, so DBAs avoided them entirely. Since PostgreSQL 10, hash indexes are WAL-logged and safe to use, but they're still rarely chosen because the B-tree's O(log N) is fast enough for almost all workloads (3–4 levels for a billion rows) and the B-tree supports a much wider range of operations. The one niche where hash indexes shine is very large equality-only lookups where the B-tree's depth becomes a concern — but in practice, B-trees scale to billions of rows comfortably, so the niche is small. Hash indexes are also used internally for hash joins and hash aggregates, but those are query-execution-time structures, not persistent indexes. For application-level indexes, default to B-tree unless you have a measured reason otherwise.
**Visual:**
```
B-tree:   sorted, O(log N), supports =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, LIKE 'x%'  (default)
Hash:     hash table, O(1) avg, supports = ONLY  (no range, no order)

B-tree at 1B rows: ~4 levels -> 4 page reads per lookup  (fast enough)
Hash:              1 lookup, but no range/order support    (rarely worth it)

Use hash only for: very large equality-only lookups (rare)
Default to B-tree for everything.
```

### Q7. What is a partial index, and when is it useful?
**Answer:** A partial index is an index that covers only rows matching a `WHERE` clause — e.g., `CREATE INDEX idx_unpaid_orders ON orders(user_id) WHERE status = 'unpaid'`. The index is smaller (only unpaid orders are indexed) and faster to scan, because the predicate is baked into the index structure. Partial indexes are useful when (a) a query always filters on a stable predicate (`WHERE active = 1`, `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`), and (b) that predicate matches a small fraction of the table. A 100M-row `users` table where only 1% are active gets a 100× smaller index for `WHERE active = 1` queries. Partial indexes are also useful for enforcing constraints on a subset of rows: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uniq_email_active ON users(email) WHERE active = 1` enforces email uniqueness only among active users, allowing multiple soft-deleted users with the same email. The trade-off is the optimizer must recognize that the query's predicate implies the index's predicate — if the query says `WHERE active = 1 AND name = 'Ada'`, the optimizer can use the partial index on `name WHERE active = 1`, but only if it can prove the implication. PostgreSQL is good at this; some engines are not.
**Visual:**
```
Full index:        CREATE INDEX ON users(email);              -- 100M entries
Partial index:     CREATE INDEX ON users(email)
                   WHERE active = 1;                          -- 1M entries (1%)
                   -- 100x smaller; 100x faster scans

Unique partial:    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email)
                   WHERE active = 1;                          -- email unique only
                   -- among active users; soft-deleted duplicates OK
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Instagram's photo-feed query is `SELECT url, caption FROM media WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Design the optimal index.
**Answer:** The optimal index is a **composite covering index** on `(user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (url, caption)` (PostgreSQL syntax) or `(user_id, created_at, url, caption)` as a composite (sqlite/MySQL emulation). The first two columns form the lookup key: `user_id` for the equality predicate, `created_at DESC` so the index is already sorted in the order the query needs (no separate sort step). The INCLUDE columns (url, caption) make it a covering index — the query can be answered entirely from the index, with no heap fetch. The execution plan is: traverse the B-tree to the leaf for `user_id = ?`, walk sideways (descending) for 20 entries, return — total ~4 I/Os (3 index pages + 0 heap), all sequential within the leaf. Without the covering property, each of the 20 rows requires a separate heap fetch (random I/O), so the covering index is roughly 5–10× faster. At Instagram's scale, this index is replicated across thousands of MySQL shards; each shard's index fits in memory. The trade-off: every photo upload must update this index (write cost), but the read savings on billions of feed queries per day dwarf the write cost.
**Visual:**
```
CREATE INDEX idx_media_feed
  ON media(user_id, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (url, caption);

Plan:
  Index Only Scan using idx_media_feed
    Index Cond: (user_id = ?)
    -> walk 20 leaves descending (already sorted, no Sort node)
    -> return url, caption from index (no heap fetch)
  Total: ~4 I/Os, all sequential.  Sub-millisecond.
```

### Q2. Your `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows 8 indexes with `idx_scan = 0` over the last 30 days. What do you do?
**Answer:** These are dead-weight indexes — they cost writes and storage but are never read. The action depends on context. First, verify the 30-day window is representative: did any monthly batch job run that might use them? Check `pg_stat_user_indexes` over a longer window (90 days) if possible. Second, check whether they enforce unique constraints — `idx_scan = 0` on a unique index used only for constraint enforcement is fine; don't drop it. Third, check whether they're used by foreign keys — PostgreSQL uses the referenced column's index for cascade deletes; dropping it can degrade FK enforcement. Fourth, for genuinely unused indexes, drop them in a maintenance window with `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (PostgreSQL), which avoids locking the table during the drop. Fifth, monitor for a week after dropping — if any query's plan regresses (a sequential scan replaced an index scan), you'll see it in `pg_stat_statements` and can recreate the index. A common gotcha: ORMs sometimes generate ad-hoc queries that use an index only on specific parameter values; an unused index might suddenly become critical when a new feature ships. The standard practice is to log the drop in a change ticket so it's easy to roll back.
**Visual:**
```
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan, idx_tup_read
  FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
 WHERE idx_scan = 0;

Check before dropping:
  - 30-day window representative?  (look at 90-day)
  - supports a UNIQUE constraint?  (don't drop)
  - supports a FOREIGN KEY?        (don't drop without alternative)

Drop:  DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_unused_foo;
       (no table lock; safe for production)
Monitor for a week; recreate if any plan regresses.
```

### Q3. A query `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'shipped'` is slow. The optimizer picks a sequential scan. What index would you add?
**Answer:** Two reasonable options: (a) a composite index on `(customer_id, status)` — optimal for this exact query, also useful for `WHERE customer_id = ?` alone (leftmost prefix). (b) A partial index on `(customer_id) WHERE status = 'shipped'` — smaller (only shipped orders indexed) and faster, but only useful if `status = 'shipped'` is a stable, common predicate. Choose (a) if `status` varies and you query multiple status values; choose (b) if you almost always filter on `status = 'shipped'` and shipped orders are a small fraction. Either way, the index turns the sequential scan into an index scan: ~3–4 I/Os instead of scanning the whole table. To make it a covering index for `SELECT *`, you'd need to INCLUDE all columns of `orders`, which is usually not worth it (the index would be as large as the table) — instead, accept the heap fetch for `SELECT *`. For `SELECT id, total` (a narrow projection), a covering index on `(customer_id, status) INCLUDE (id, total)` gives an index-only scan. After creating the index, verify with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` that the plan switched to Index Scan and the runtime dropped.
**Visual:**
```
Slow: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42 AND status='shipped';
       -> Seq Scan (cost=0..154)  -- 30 seconds on 100M rows

Option A (composite):    CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id, status);
                         -> Index Scan (cost=0.42..8.45)  -- milliseconds

Option B (partial):      CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id)
                         WHERE status = 'shipped';
                         -> smaller index; only useful if 'shipped' is the common case

Covering (narrow proj):  CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id, status) INCLUDE (id, total);
                         -> Index-Only Scan for SELECT id, total FROM ...
```

### Q4. Your write-heavy metrics table receives 100k INSERTs/sec. Adding a 4th index slows inserts by 40%. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** Write-heavy tables are where indexing trade-offs bite hardest. First, **measure which indexes are actually used** via `pg_stat_user_indexes`; drop any that aren't (this happens — indexes accumulate over time as queries change). Second, **consider whether the 4th index can be a partial index** — if the query is `WHERE metric = 'cpu' AND ts > now() - interval '1 hour'`, a partial index `WHERE metric = 'cpu'` halves the index size and write cost. Third, **batch inserts** — instead of 100k single-row INSERTs, batch into 1k-row multi-value inserts; this amortizes per-statement overhead and the index update cost. Fourth, **defer indexing with the outbox pattern** — write metrics to a buffer table with no secondary indexes, then a background worker batches and re-inserts into the indexed table. Fifth, **use a time-series database** (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) for metrics — they're optimized for high-write time-series workloads with chunked indexes. Sixth, **partition the table** by time (daily or hourly) — each partition's index is smaller, fits in memory, and updates are confined to the active partition. The right answer depends on the query pattern; for pure time-series, partition + TimescaleDB is usually correct.
**Visual:**
```
100k inserts/sec + 4 indexes -> 40% slower

Options:
  1. Audit indexes: pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan=0  -> DROP
  2. Partial index: WHERE metric='cpu'  (smaller, less write cost)
  3. Batch inserts: 100k single-row -> 100 multi-row of 1k each
  4. Outbox: buffer table (no 2nd idx) -> background worker -> indexed table
  5. Time-series DB: TimescaleDB / InfluxDB (chunked, write-optimized)
  6. Partition by time: each partition's index smaller; updates confined
```

### Q5. Your `users` table has 100M rows. The query `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE active = 1` takes 5 minutes. How do you speed it up?
**Answer:** `COUNT(*)` with a predicate is a notorious slow query because most databases must actually count matching rows — there's no constant-time shortcut. Options, in order of practicality: (1) **Index-only scan** — `CREATE INDEX ON users(active) INCLUDE (id)` (or just `CREATE INDEX ON users(active)`); with the visibility map clean, PostgreSQL can count from the index without touching the heap, often 10× faster. (2) **Partial index** — `CREATE INDEX ON users(id) WHERE active = 1`; then `SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE active = 1` uses the partial index, which is much smaller (only active rows). (3) **Materialized view** — if exact count isn't needed, maintain a `user_stats` table updated by triggers; queries read the cached count in microseconds. (4) **Approximate count** — if "approximately 50M active users" is acceptable, use PostgreSQL's `pg_class.reltuples` (updated by ANALYZE) for a fast estimate, or run a `TABLESAMPLE` query. (5) **Counter table** — maintain `daily_active_counts` updated by application code or triggers; this is what social networks do for "X active users today" displays. The right answer depends on freshness requirements: real-time exact → counter table; near-real-time → materialized view; approximate → pg_class.
**Visual:**
```
Slow:    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE active=1;  -- 5min, scans 100M rows

Faster:
  (1) Index-only scan:    CREATE INDEX ON users(active);  -- visibility map clean
                          -> Index Only Scan, 10x faster
  (2) Partial index:      CREATE INDEX ON users(id) WHERE active=1;
                          -> scans only active rows (1M instead of 100M)
  (3) Materialized view:  user_stats(active_count) refreshed by triggers
                          -> microseconds, but slightly stale
  (4) Approximate:        SELECT reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname='users';
                          -> instant, ~1% accurate
  (5) Counter table:      daily_active_counts updated async; what social nets use
```

### Q6. You have `WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01' AND status = 'paid'` on a 500M-row table. The composite index `(created_at, status)` isn't being used. Why?
**Answer:** Most likely a statistics issue: the optimizer estimates the predicate matches too many rows (e.g., >20%) and picks a sequential scan instead. The first diagnostic is `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` — look at the estimated vs actual row counts. If the estimate is way off (estimate 100M, actual 5M), run `ANALYZE orders` to refresh statistics. The second possibility is the index isn't selective enough for the leading column: `created_at >= '2024-01-01'` might match 10M rows (one month out of years), and the optimizer might think a bitmap scan on the index plus recheck is too expensive. The third possibility is data correlation: if `status` is correlated with `created_at` (e.g., older orders are mostly `paid`, newer are mostly `pending`), the optimizer's independence assumption misestimates the combined selectivity — fix with extended statistics (`CREATE STATISTICS` on `(created_at, status)`). The fourth possibility is the index column order: if `status` is queried equally often, `(status, created_at)` might be better. The fifth is that the index exists but is bloated (dead tuples inflate page count) — run `pg_repack` to rebuild it. After ruling out statistics, try `(status, created_at)` or extended stats.
**Visual:**
```
Query: WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-02-01' AND status='paid'
Index: (created_at, status)  exists but not used.

Diagnose with EXPLAIN ANALYZE:
  estimated rows = 100M, actual rows = 5M  -> STATISTICS problem -> ANALYZE
  estimated rows = 5M, actual rows = 5M, but Seq Scan chosen
    -> optimizer thinks 5M is too many for index scan (>20% threshold)

Fixes:
  1. ANALYZE orders;                       (refresh stats)
  2. CREATE STATISTICS ON created_at, status;  (capture correlation)
  3. Try (status, created_at) order        (if status is more selective)
  4. pg_repack to rebuild bloated index
  5. SET enable_seqscan = off;             (test only, to force index)
```

### Q7. Your team added an index in production and it didn't speed up the query — the optimizer still chose a sequential scan. Why might this happen?
**Answer:** Several possibilities. (1) **Statistics stale** — the optimizer doesn't know the new index exists with current statistics; run `ANALYZE tablename`. (2) **Wrong column order** — you created `(status, customer_id)` but the query is `WHERE customer_id = ?`; the leftmost-prefix rule means the index can't be used because the leading column (`status`) isn't in the predicate. (3) **Predicate too unselective** — the optimizer correctly determined the index scan would be slower than a sequential scan because the predicate matches >20% of rows; the index isn't useful for this query. (4) **Function on the indexed column** — `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'ada@x.com'` can't use an index on `email` (the function defeats the B-tree's sort order); you need a functional index `CREATE INDEX ON users(LOWER(email))`. (5) **Type mismatch** — `WHERE user_id = '42'` (string) on an `INTEGER` column prevents index use because the cast changes the comparison semantics; fix the query to use the right type. (6) **Index is bloated or corrupt** — reindex. (7) **The optimizer cost model is wrong** — set `enable_seqscan = off` temporarily to force the index and confirm it's faster; if so, the cost constants (`random_page_cost`, `cpu_index_tuple_cost`) may need tuning. The diagnostic is always `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.
**Visual:**
```
Index added but optimizer still picks Seq Scan. Causes:

  1. ANALYZE not run after CREATE INDEX -> run ANALYZE tablename
  2. Wrong column order: index (status, customer_id), query WHERE customer_id=?
     -> leftmost prefix not satisfied; recreate as (customer_id, status)
  3. Predicate >20% of rows -> index scan slower than seq scan (correct choice)
  4. Function on column: WHERE LOWER(email)=?  -> index on email unusable
     -> CREATE INDEX ON users(LOWER(email))  (functional index)
  5. Type mismatch: WHERE user_id='42' on INTEGER col -> cast prevents index
  6. Bloat -> REINDEX
  7. Cost model wrong -> SET enable_seqscan=off; test; tune random_page_cost
```

quiz.explanation: bitmap scan** is a two-phase index access: first, the index lookup produces a bitmap of tuple IDs matching the predicate (one bit per page, or per tuple, depending on precision); second, the heap fetches are done in page-number order, converting random I/O into mostly-sequential I/O. There are two variants: Bitmap Index Scan (builds the bitmap) and Bitmap Heap Scan (fetches the pages in sorted order).
